content.text: Eid-Ul-Fitr (~) is the Festival of Breaking the Fast, celebrated on the first day of Shawwal, the tenth month of the Islamic calendar. It marks the joyous conclusion of Ramadan's month-long fasting. This is one of the two major celebrations in Islam, alongside Eid al-Adha.The name "Eid al-Fitr" translates to "Festival of Breaking the Fast." It's a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete Ramadan and for the spiritual growth achieved during the blessed month.On this day, Muslims gather for a special congregational prayer in the morning, give obligatory charity called Zakat al-Fitr, wear their finest clothes, and celebrate with family and friends. Children often receive gifts and new clothes. Special foods and sweets are prepared across Muslim communities worldwide.Before the Eid prayer, every Muslim who has the means must pay Zakat al-Fitr. This ensures that even the poorest can celebrate with dignity and joy.Eid-Ul-Fitr (~) 2026 in United StatesEid-Ul-Fitr (~) in United States for 2026 is expected to fall on March 20, corresponding to 1 Shawwal 1447 in the Islamic calendar.The exact date depends on the sighting of the new crescent moon that marks the end of Ramadan.See the full calendar in the appBest Premium Offer — Only on Web Limited Time Offer!Remove ads. Get real-time Adhan alerts, track your ibadah, ask our AI assistant, and stay inspired every step of the way.The Islamic CalendarThe Hijri Calendar: A Lunar SystemThe Islamic calendar, also known as the Hijri calendar (1446 AH), is based on the phases of the moon, unlike the solar-based Gregorian calendar. Its starting point is the Hijrah, which was the Prophet Muhammad's migration to Medina. A new month officially begins when the new moon is sighted at the close of the previous month. Because the start of each month depends on this lunar sighting, the calendar provides an estimated, rather than a fixed, schedule for upcoming Islamic dates.Calendar Structure and MonthsLike the Gregorian calendar, the Islamic year has 12 months. However, it is shorter, with each year containing approximately 354 to 355 days compared to the 365 or 366 days of the Gregorian calendar. The months in order are: Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi al-Thani, Jumada al-Awwal, Jumada al-Thani, Rajab, Shaban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qadah, and Dhul Hijjah.Sacred MonthsFour months in the Islamic calendar are considered sacred, and it's forbidden to wage war during them. As stated in a narration from the Prophet (PBUH) found in Bukhari (3197), these months are: 'Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah, and Muharram, which occur in succession, and the fourth is Rajab.'Important Events and Online ResourcesKey Islamic holidays and major events, such as Eid al-Fitr, Hajj, and Eid al-Adha, are determined by the dates of the Hijri calendar. The Muslim Pro app and website provides these dates, which allow you to easily convert dates between the Hijri and Gregorian systems. Many of these resources let you view both calendars side-by-side for convenience.
